stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with 8 weeks of dry cough. Never smoker. No wheeze. On ramipril for 5 years. CXR is normal. She has tried saline nasal spray without change.

parts.q: List the FOUR most likely causes to consider for her chronic cough.
parts.marks: Any 4. The big three (upper airway, asthma, reflux) plus ACE-inhibitor cough, in a non-smoker with a normal CXR. Cancer/TB/heart failure are not the leading causes in this low-risk profile but are considered if the trial-of-therapy approach fails.

parts.q: Outline the next TWO steps in management.
options: Stop or switch the ramipril (e.g., to an ARB) and review in 2-4 weeks
Sequential trial of therapy for the likely cause(s): intranasal steroid and/or asthma therapy and/or PPI, reviewed at defined intervals
parts.marks: ACE cessation first (up to 4 weeks to assess), then empirical sequential trials per the likely cause. Imaging if red flags appear or trials fail; opioids are not management.

stem: A 72-year-old man has recurrent brief dizziness on rolling over in bed and on looking up, each lasting under a minute, with nausea. No hearing loss, no headache. Cardiovascular exam and neurology are normal.

parts.q: What is the MOST likely diagnosis, and list the TWO features that best support it.
options: Brief episodes (seconds) provoked by specific head-position change
parts.marks: BPPV: seconds-long, positionally triggered (rolling in bed, looking up), no auditory/neuro features. Meniere = hours + hearing loss; VBI = neuro signs; vestibular migraine = minutes-hours + migraine.

parts.q: List the THREE most appropriate management steps.
options: Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre to confirm (with observation for positional nystagmus)
Epley manoeuvre (canalith repositioning) - can be performed in the practice
Referral to neurology in all cases
parts.marks: Confirm with Dix-Hallpike, treat with Epley (often curative on the spot), reassure. Chronic suppressants (prochlorperazine) delay compensation and are not maintenance; imaging only for atypical features.

stem: An 84-year-old woman has lost 8 kg over 6 months. She lives alone, has early dementia (MMSE 23/30), takes 8 medications, and has poor dentition. She seems cheerful but thin (BMI 19).

parts.q: List the SIX most important contributors to assess.
options: Medication side-effects (nausea, dry mouth, sedation, appetite loss)
Cognitive contribution: forgetting meals, shopping, cooking
Systemic disease screen (malignancy, thyrotoxicosis, infection, malabsorption)
parts.marks: Any 6 of the first 6. In the elderly weight loss is usually multifactorial: mechanical (teeth, swallow), psychiatric (depression), iatrogenic (drugs), functional (dementia), plus occult disease - each needs a screen. Menopause and eating disorders are not the drivers here.

parts.q: List the FOUR most appropriate initial investigations.
options: Colonoscopy for all elderly weight loss
parts.marks: Any 4. First-line systemic screen: FBE, UEC/LFT/Ca, TSH, inflammatory markers, CXR. Tumour markers are NOT screening tests (low specificity, no proven role); imaging/endoscopy is targeted by findings.

unit: Population health and the context of general practice
stem: A 52-year-old man attends for a health assessment. He has not seen a GP for 5 years. Smokes 15/day, BMI 31, BP 148/92 (repeated), drinks 30 standard drinks/week. No meds. No significant family history.

parts.q: List the SIX most appropriate preventive assessments/interventions for this visit.
options: Annual whole-body skin checks for everyone
parts.marks: Any 6 of the first 6. This visit packs: CVD risk (age+smoking+BP), BP management, two brief interventions (smoking, alcohol), diabetes screen (obesity), and bowel program participation. PSA is informed-choice only; whole-body checks are not recommended.

parts.q: His absolute CVD risk returns 12% (moderate). List the FOUR management elements you discuss.
options: Lifestyle plan: smoking, alcohol, diet, activity (moderate risk = aggressive lifestyle first with review)
BP management: confirm with home readings, consider therapy if sustained >=140/90 after lifestyle attempt
Statins NOT automatic at 12% - discuss individual factors and preferences
parts.marks: Any 4 of the first 4. Moderate risk: intensive lifestyle with structured review; treat BP if confirmed; statin discussion is individualised (not automatic at moderate risk but considered with additional factors). Neither reflex statin nor reflex dismissal.

stem: A 31-year-old G1P0 at 9 weeks presents to establish antenatal care. She is well, takes folic acid, is immune to rubella, and has a normal BMI. Her partner is from a country with high hepatitis B prevalence.

parts.q: List the SIX routine antenatal screening tests appropriate at booking (first trimester).
parts.marks: Any 6 of the first 6. Booking bloods: group/antibodies, FBE, hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis; plus urine MC&S. (Hep C per risk, VZV if uncertain, chlamydia per risk.) Invasive tests and toxo serology are not routine Australian booking tests.

parts.q: List the FOUR additional assessments/actions for her specifically.
options: Chlamydia screening (per guidelines - offer to all pregnant women <30 or per risk)
Offer NIPT/cfDNA discussion or combined first-trimester screening (11-13+6 weeks) as per her choice
Folic acid continuation to 12 weeks; iodine supplementation advice
parts.marks: Any 4. Partner risk (Hep B household risk) informs additional screening; STI screen; discuss Down syndrome screening options early (window 11-13+6); folic acid/iodine. Steroids are 24-34 weeks preterm; anti-D is 28 weeks (Rh-negative only) or with sensitising events.

stem: A 33-year-old mother of a 10-week-old presents with the baby for a check. You notice she is flat, avoids eye contact, and mentions the baby 'cries all night'. Partner works away. EPDS today is 16.

parts.q: List the FOUR most important components of assessment.
options: Direct suicide risk assessment (thoughts, plan, means, intent)
Assessment of bonding/attachment and any thoughts of harm to the baby
Supports at home (partner availability, family, sleep)
Sleep, appetite and severity of depression symptoms
parts.marks: Any 4 of first 4. PND assessment: risk to self, risk to/bonding with baby, supports, symptom severity. (TSH if clinical suspicion only; admission is for risk/psychosis/severe impairment, not a score alone.)

parts.q: List the FIVE most appropriate management steps.
options: Safety plan and rapid follow-up (within days)
Referral for perinatal psychological therapy (e.g., through a perinatal mental health pathway)
SSRI discussion if moderate-severe, with breastfeeding-compatible choices (e.g., sertraline)
Engage partner/family supports (with consent) including practical night help
MCH nurse/child health follow-up and GP review scheduled
parts.marks: Any 5 of the first 5. Multimodal: safety, therapy, medication where indicated (breastfeeding-compatible), practical/social supports, structured follow-up. Never stop breastfeeding as 'treatment'; no long-term benzos.

stem: A 47-year-old man has 3 years of low back pain following an injury at work. MRI shows mild multi-level disc degeneration, no neural compression. He takes oxycodone 40 mg/day (prescribed elsewhere), reports poor sleep and low mood, and has stopped working.

parts.q: List the FOUR key elements of a biopsychosocial assessment here.
options: Pain behaviour and flare pattern; function (what he avoids)
Mood, sleep, catastrophising and beliefs about pain
Work, compensation and litigation context; social supports
Medication review: opioid dose, effectiveness, harms, other sedatives
Urine drug screening for all patients as a first step
parts.marks: Any 4 of the first 4. Chronic pain assessment is biopsychosocial: function, mood/sleep/beliefs, context (work/compensation), and a structured medication review. Repeat imaging without new neurology adds nothing; urine screening is for clinical indication, not blanket first step.

parts.q: List the FIVE most appropriate management steps.
options: Gradual opioid taper plan with support (never abrupt cessation)
Enrol in an interdisciplinary pain program (e.g., ADAPT-style) or pain psychologist
Sleep and mood management (CBT-I principles; treat depression)
Address work capacity/vocational rehabilitation with insurer
parts.marks: Any 5 of the first 5. Chronic pain: taper (high-dose opioids worsen outcomes), interdisciplinary program, mood/sleep, pacing and graded return to work. Escalating opioids, adding benzos, or fusion without specific indication are the classic wrong answers.

unit: Migrant, refugee and asylum seeker health
stem: A 28-year-old woman recently arrived from a refugee settlement in Africa attends for a health assessment. She speaks no English, is 14 weeks pregnant (first antenatal), and has never had bloods.

parts.q: List the FOUR most important immediate system actions.
options: Book a professional interpreter (TIS National) for all clinical discussions
Establish antenatal care pathway (booking bloods, gestation dating)
Screen for common refugee health issues: hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis exposure
Mental health screen (trauma-informed; do not force disclosure), with awareness of torture/trauma prevalence
parts.marks: Any 4 of the first 4. Professional interpreter (never family), start antenatal care, refugee health screening bundle, and trauma-informed mental health approach. Family interpreters breach confidentiality and accuracy.

parts.q: List the FOUR key components of the refugee health screen relevant to her.
options: Hepatitis B serology (prevalence high; vaccinate if susceptible)
Tuberculosis screen (IGRA/CXR safe in pregnancy, no live vaccines now)
Parasite screen if eosinophilia (e.g., strongyloides serology, schistosoma if from an endemic region)
parts.marks: Any 4 of first 4. Pregnancy-safe screening bundle: hep B, HIV/syphilis, TB (IGRA/CXR), parasites (strongyloides/schistosoma per geography, esp. Africa). Live vaccines (MMR/varicella) are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy - postpartum.

stem: You are the GP for a 29-year-old intern who discloses 3 months of exhaustion, night-shift sleep chaos, low mood and a growing dread of work. He admits to taking zopiclone from a sample pack and drinking 6+ standard drinks to sleep. No suicidal ideation. He is terrified of anyone finding out.

parts.q: List the FOUR most important elements of your management.
options: Treat him as any patient: structured mental health assessment (severity, risk, alcohol review)
Encourage registration with his own GP and the doctors' health service (confidential, not reportable)
Practical work plan discussion: rosters, sleep protection, speaking with DCT/supervisor if and when he consents
Clear plan for zopiclone/alcohol: safer sleep strategy, short review interval
Inform his training program without consent
parts.marks: Any 4 of the first 4. Confidential care with risk assessment; doctors' health services; consent-based workplace steps; address the sedative/alcohol spiral. Reporting is for impaired practice risking the public - not for seeking treatment (treating-doctor exemption).

parts.q: Which THREE principles underpin safe care for doctor-patients?
options: Encourage a treating team separate from workplace (own GP, doctors' health service)
Early intervention prevents both patient harm and public risk
parts.marks: Any 3. Same confidentiality, separate treaters, early help. Self-prescribing and informal colleague care are the twin failures of doctors' health.

unit: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
stem: A 52-year-old Aboriginal man attends with tiredness. He has not had a health check for years. HbA1c returns 7.2% (new diabetes). He mentions his father died of 'sugar and kidney trouble'. He is wary of hospitals after his father's experience.

parts.q: List the FOUR most important elements of today's consultation.
options: Ask how he would like his care organised (choice of services, including ATSI community-controlled options)
Confirm diabetes diagnosis and explain it plainly, linking to family history
715 health check to structure comprehensive care (CTG entitlements)
Book follow-up soon with a defined plan - relationship over transaction
Send a letter to the hospital diabetes clinic today
Discount his father's experience as irrelevant
parts.marks: Any 4. Patient-led service choices; plain-language diagnosis + family history connection; 715 anchor; early follow-up builds trust (did not attend clinics reflect system failure, not patient failure). His father's story shapes his engagement - it must be heard.

parts.q: List the FOUR key management steps for his new type 2 diabetes.
options: Explain diagnosis + confirm (repeat if asymptomatic per guidelines)
Arrange cycle-of-care: retinal, ACR, eGFR, feet, BP, lipids
Start metformin with lifestyle (or discuss per guidelines and preference)
Annual flu + pneumococcal + hepatitis B vaccination review
Daily home glucose monitoring for life
parts.marks: Any 4 of first 4. Confirm and classify; full complication screen; metformin + lifestyle as the base; vaccination review (diabetes = risk group). Insulin and lifelong SMBG are not first steps; 'wait and see' risks complications given family history.

stem: A 34-year-old hairdresser has 8 months of hand dermatitis: scaling, fissures and itch on both palms and fingerwebs, worse at work, marginally better on weekends. Patch testing shows allergy to a hair dye component and an irritant component from shampoos.

parts.q: What is the MOST likely diagnosis and the TWO contributing mechanisms?
parts.marks: Occupational contact dermatitis with BOTH allergic (hair dye) and irritant (wet work) mechanisms - common in hairdressers. Favouring work/weekend pattern supports occupational causation.

parts.q: List the FIVE most appropriate management steps.
options: Detailed advice on allergen avoidance (dye component) and reading product labels
Wet-work reduction: gloves, drying regime, soap substitution
Potent topical corticosteroid for flare control then stepping down
WorkCover notification and occupational assessment (causation has compensation implications)
parts.marks: Any 5 of first 5. Allergen avoidance + wet-work reduction + topical therapy + emollients + occupational notification (compensation and workplace modification). Systemic immunosuppression is not the answer; abrupt career advice ignores modification options.

stem: A 17-year-old competitive rower attends for a sports medical before the season. He mentions one episode of near-syncope at the end of an intense session last month, and his uncle died suddenly at 40 while exercising.

parts.q: List the FOUR key elements of assessment.
options: Family history detail (uncle's death circumstances, any <50 SCD) - pre-participation screen red flag
Exertional near-syncope history: triggers, timing, symptoms
Cardiovascular examination incl. BP, murmur (HOCM), radial/femoral pulses (coarctation)
ECG as part of the screening pathway
Exercise stress test in the practice
parts.marks: Any 4 of first 4. Exertional presyncope + family SCD = red flags: examine, ECG, and refer; history-taking is the highest-yield screen. In-practice stress testing is not the first move.

parts.q: What is the MOST appropriate referral pathway and the TWO reasons?
options: Urgent cardiology/sports-medicine referral before he returns to competition
Exertional symptoms + family history of sudden death warrant specialist evaluation before clearance
A normal ECG alone cannot exclude underlying cardiac disease
parts.marks: Any 3. Referral pre-clearance because exertional syncope + SCD family history is a recognised red-flag combination; a normal surface ECG does not fully exclude cardiomyopathy/channelopathy - further evaluation (echo, ambulatory ECG, sometimes MRI) is specialist-led.

stem: A 22-year-old woman discloses she was sexually assaulted by an acquaintance last night. She is tearful, has not told anyone, and asks what her options are. She does not want police involvement at this stage.

parts.q: List the FOUR most important immediate actions.
options: Immediate medical needs: injuries assessed; emergency contraception discussion (time window)
Acute psychological care: trauma-informed approach, belief, control back to her
STI prophylaxis and baseline testing (with follow-up plan) - per protocols
Forensic option explained WITHOUT pressure: sexual assault service can collect and store evidence even if she has not decided about police
Insist she reports to police before any care
Call the police without her consent
Ask her to recount every detail for the record
parts.marks: Any 4 of first 4. Care before forensics: treat, protect (EC/STI), support - and inform her the forensic window exists with a service that can store evidence while she decides. Police reporting is HER choice (reporting obligations vary by jurisdiction but care never waits).

parts.q: List the FOUR elements of follow-up.
options: Scheduled early review (days) - trauma responses evolve
Safety assessment: does the assailant have access; is she safe where she stays
Clear documentation of her account in her words (may support later proceedings if she chooses)
parts.marks: Any 4. Early structured review, safety planning, counselling, verbatim contemporaneous documentation. Routine sedation displaces proper trauma care; involving family without consent breaches her control.

stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic knee pain asks you to take over his oxycodone prescribing from another practice. Records show escalating doses and early scripts over 18 months. He plays cricket and has two teenage kids.

parts.q: List the FOUR most appropriate steps before any prescribing decision.
options: Full pain assessment (cause, function, what has/has not helped)
Opioid risk assessment (validated tool, aberrant behaviours) and urine drug screen where indicated
Obtain records/releases from the previous prescriber
A written treatment agreement with one prescriber/pharmacy and review intervals
Prescribe the same dose immediately to maintain trust
Refuse and discharge him from the practice
Never ask about his prescribing history
parts.marks: Any 4 of first 4. Before taking over opioid therapy: assess pain and risk, verify history (records, PDMP where available), set a single-prescriber agreement with review. Blanket continuation or abrupt refusal both fail the patient.

parts.q: He asks for a dose increase because 'nothing works'. List the FOUR best responses.
options: Explain opioid-induced hyperalgesia and loss of efficacy at high doses - more is not better
Offer a structured non-opioid plan: interdisciplinary pain program, physio, mood/sleep care
Propose a slow taper with him in control, scheduled reviews and support
Treat what is actually driving pain behaviour (sleep, mood, function, context)
Increase the dose to be therapeutic
Add a second opioid for synergy
Oxycodone IR PRN on top of his current dose
parts.marks: Any 4 of the first 4. Escalation is the trap: explain hyperalgesia, build the non-drug plan, negotiate a supported taper, treat comorbid drivers. Adjunct opioids are the wrong direction.

stem: Public health notifies you that a 19-year-old patient of your practice has invasive meningococcal disease (serogroup B). His 16-year-old brother is your patient and attended today asking for 'the antibiotic'.

parts.q: What is the recommended prophylaxis for a close household contact, and list the TWO other key actions?
options: Single-dose ciprofloxacin 500 mg oral (or per current guidelines) as soon as possible
Provide clear safety-net advice: urgent care if fever/rash/illness in the next days
Confirm vaccination status - Men ACWY and Men B immunisation per schedule/risk
parts.marks: Any 3. Chemoprophylaxis ASAP (single-dose ciprofloxacin/rifampicin per guidelines), safety-netting for the incubation window, and vaccination review (Men B for serogroup B; Men ACWY per schedule). Antibiotic courses and isolation are not prophylaxis.

parts.q: List the THREE public-health responsibilities of the practice.
options: Public health manages contact identification - cooperate promptly with the notification process
Ensure household and close contacts receive timely prophylaxis information
Maintain accurate records to support contact tracing
Prescribe prophylaxis to every patient on the books
parts.marks: Any 3. Coordinate with public health, ensure contacts get timely prophylaxis, keep records supporting tracing. Mass prophylaxis/media/panic are not part of the response.
